checked_sources: Wikipedia 'Spherical harmonics' (Laplace's spherical harmonics section) - for the r^l / r^-(l+1) radial solutions and the vanish-at-infinity choice
Hallez H et al. (2007) Review on solving the forward problem in EEG source analysis, J NeuroEng Rehabil 4:46, PMC2234413 (Europe PMC full-text XML) - for the scalp-air boundary condition
Nunez, Nunez & Srinivasan 2019 - bioRxiv preprint full text 10.1101/391318v2 (journal version paywalled; Europe PMC record for bibliographic details; eScholarship record)
Jackson 3rd ed. - publisher table of contents only (Wiley listing via campus bookstore page); book text not online
Own numerical check: Legendre expansion of a 2.2 cm half-width scalp pattern on a 9.3 cm sphere, on-axis exterior decay sum a_l (R/r)^(l+1)
evidence_location: Wikipedia: separation of variables, 'R(r) = A r^l + B r^-l-1' and footnote 'Physical applications often take the solution that vanishes at infinity, making A = 0'. Hallez 2007: section 'Poisson's equation, boundary conditions and dipoles', text before eq. (11)-(12) (homogeneous Neumann condition at the head surface). Nunez 2019 preprint: Section 8.5 only says the scalp potential is 'uniquely determined by Laplace's equation given the dura potential (lower boundary condition)'; the words air, insulator (in this sense), Neumann, normal current do not occur. Jackson 3rd ed. TOC: 3.1 Laplace Equation in Spherical Coordinates, 3.2 Legendre Equation and Legendre Polynomials, 3.3 Boundary-Value Problems with Azimuthal Symmetry. Numerical check (R = 9.3 cm): Gaussian with half-width-at-half-maximum 2.2 cm gives 71% at 0.5 cm, 53% at 1 cm, 21% at 3 cm; Gaussian with sigma = 2.2 cm gives 75%, 57%, 26%; a compact raised-cosine bump of radius 2.2 cm gives 53%, 31%, 8%.
quote: no current can be injected into the air outside the human head due to the very low conductivity
discrepancy: Physics (a) and arithmetic (c) hold: exterior Laplace solutions regular at infinity are r^-(l+1) terms, and the site's 70% / ~50% / 25% at 0.5 / 1 / 3 cm match an independent calculation to within a few points (71/53/21% for a Gaussian of HWHM 2.2 cm; 75/57/26% if 2.2 cm is the Gaussian sigma) - the 3 cm value is the most shape-sensitive (8% for a compact bump that is zero beyond 2.2 cm). Attribution problem for (b): the cited Nunez, Nunez & Srinivasan 2019 text (preprint version searched in full) does not state that air is an insulator / that the normal current at the scalp vanishes; it only invokes Laplace's equation with the dura potential as lower boundary condition. The standard EEG boundary condition is stated explicitly in Hallez et al. 2007 (J Neuroeng Rehabil 4:46, open access) and in electrodynamics texts. Jackson's actual section text could not be viewed; only the section title/numbering was verified.
suggested_fix: Keep the physics wording. For the 'air as insulator, no current leaves the head' boundary condition cite a source that states it, e.g. Hallez H, Vanrumste B, Grech R et al. (2007) Review on solving the forward problem in EEG source analysis. J NeuroEngineering Rehabil 4:46, doi:10.1186/1743-0003-4-46 (or Nunez & Srinivasan, Electric Fields of the Brain, 2006), and cite Nunez 2019 only for the general volume-conduction framing. State the assumed head radius and the profile shape (e.g. Gaussian, half-width at half-maximum 2.2 cm) next to the percentages, since the 3 cm figure moves between ~20% and ~26% for Gaussians and much lower for compact bumps.
bibliographic_issues: Nunez PL, Nunez MD, Srinivasan R (2019) Brain Topography 32(2):193-214, doi:10.1007/s10548-019-00701-3 - all details match Europe PMC and eScholarship records. Jackson 3rd edition (Wiley, 1999) Sect. 3.3 title 'Boundary-Value Problems with Azimuthal Symmetry' matches the publisher's table of contents (ISBN 9780471309321).

checked_sources: Huigen, Peper & Grimbergen 2002 - abstract only (Springer article page, Europe PMC record, Amsterdam UMC Pure record); full text paywalled, no open copy via Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/CORE/UvA-DARE
Kappenman & Luck 2010 - full text PDF (author copy at erpinfo.org), incl. Figure 4 rendered and inspected

Secondary witness only: Chi YM, Jung TP, Cauwenberghs G (2010) Dry-contact and noncontact biopotential electrodes: methodological review, IEEE Rev Biomed Eng 3:106-119, p. 116 (PDF from isn.ucsd.edu), which cites Huigen for a 1/f characteristic
evidence_location: Huigen abstract: 'Depending on skin treatment, magnitudes between 1 and 20 microVrms were measured among subjects'; 'noise mainly originates in the electrolyte-skin interface'; 'highly dependent on the electrode gel used and the skin properties'; 'inversely proportional to the square root of the area of the electrode on the skin'. Kappenman & Luck: Abstract ('Low-frequency noise was found to be increased at high-impedance sites relative to low-impedance sites, especially when the recording environment was warm and humid'); Method p. 891-892 (one hemisphere abraded to <5 kOhm, other left unabraded at 10-190 kOhm); Results p. 895-896 and Figure 4 ('amplitude density was similar across conditions for the higher frequencies (10-100 Hz) but differed in the lower frequencies'; in Fig. 4 the high-impedance curves separate from the low-impedance curves below roughly 5-10 Hz and overlap above ~10 Hz). Chi 2010 review p. 116: noise 'far exceeds the amount predicted by thermal noise at low frequencies [4]' and 'the redox reaction at the electrode accounts for the 1/f characteristic with wet Ag/AgCl electrodes [4]' where [4] = Huigen 2002.
quote: Depending on skin treatment, magnitudes between 1 and 20 microVrms were measured among subjects
discrepancy: Verified from Huigen's abstract: the 1-20 uV rms range, its dependence on skin treatment, the electrolyte-skin origin and the 1/sqrt(area) scaling. NOT verifiable from the accessible text: (i) the 1/f spectrum - not in the abstract; only corroborated second-hand by Chi et al. 2010, which attributes a '1/f characteristic' to Huigen; (ii) the explicit direction 'lower for prepared skin' - the abstract says only 'depending on skin treatment' (the direction is physically expected and consistent with Kappenman & Luck, who found less low-frequency noise at abraded sites, but Huigen's wording could not be seen); (iii) the measurement bandwidth - not given in the abstract. Nuance dropped: Huigen's 1-20 uV rms range was measured with gelled (electrolyte) electrodes, so the site's dry-plate and plate-over-hair values (8 uV) are extrapolations beyond that source, not values 'placed within' a measured dry-electrode range. Kappenman & Luck support higher low-frequency noise at unabraded high-impedance sites; the paper's text contrasts '10-100 Hz' (similar) with 'lower frequencies' (different) and gives no '5 Hz' figure - 'below ~5 Hz' is a reading of Figure 4, not a stated number.
suggested_fix: Say: 'Huigen et al. measured 1-20 uV rms for gelled electrodes depending on skin treatment, with noise scaling as 1/sqrt(electrode area); the 1/f shape and the values for dry plates and plates over hair are modelling assumptions (the 1/f character of wet-electrode noise is attributed to Huigen by Chi et al. 2010).' For Kappenman & Luck say 'noise elevated at low frequencies (spectra similar above ~10 Hz)' rather than quoting 5 Hz, unless the 5 Hz is explicitly labelled as read from their Figure 4. If the bandwidth matters, obtain the Huigen full text before stating one.
bibliographic_issues: Huigen E, Peper A, Grimbergen CA (2002) Med Biol Eng Comput 40(3):332-338, doi:10.1007/BF02344216 - matches Europe PMC/OpenAlex. Kappenman ES, Luck SJ (2010) Psychophysiology 47(5):888-904, doi:10.1111/j.1469-8986.2010.01009.x - matches the PDF header (vol 47, pp. 888-904, DOI) and Europe PMC (issue 5). No bibliographic errors.

checked_sources: Chi, Maier & Cauwenberghs 2011 - abstract and bibliographic record (IEEE Xplore record 6122459 via a library catalog mirror, bvbvf1.bib-bvb.de; Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex metadata). IEEE Xplore page itself blocked; full body text not accessed (paywalled, no open copy)
Context: Texas Instruments ADS1299 datasheet SBAS499C (July 2012, revised January 2017), downloaded from ti.com and read with pdftotext
evidence_location: Chi et al. 2011 abstract: custom integrated noncontact front-end amplifier; 'Input impedance (no neutralization): 60 fF || 50 TOhm'; 'input referred noise: 0.05 fA/sqrt(Hz) and 200 nV/sqrt(Hz) at 1 Hz'; 1.5 uA per channel at 3.3 V; stable below 0.05 Hz with coupling capacitances down to 0.5 pF. ADS1299 datasheet: Electrical Characteristics table, 'Input bias current ... +/-300 pA' (typ, 25 C), 'DC input impedance 1000 MOhm' (no lead-off; 500 MOhm with current-source lead-off); section 9.3.1.3: 'The ADS1299-x has CMOS inputs and therefore has negligible current noise.' No input current-noise density is specified anywhere in the datasheet.
discrepancy: Both attributed numbers appear verbatim in the abstract and the journal/volume/issue/pages/DOI all match. Minor nuance: in the abstract the qualifier 'at 1 Hz' follows both noise figures, so the 0.05 fA/sqrt(Hz) current noise is also a 1 Hz spot value, not a broadband figure; the site attaches 'at 1 Hz' only to the voltage noise. Context for the 1 fA/sqrt(Hz) default: the ADS1299 datasheet gives no current-noise figure, only +/-300 pA typical input bias current and the qualitative statement 'negligible current noise'. If that 300 pA leakage carried full shot noise, sqrt(2qI) would be about 10 fA/sqrt(Hz) (auditor's own calculation, not a datasheet value), i.e. an order of magnitude above the slider default; so 1 fA/sqrt(Hz) should be presented as an assumption rather than as typical of a commercial front end.
suggested_fix: Write '0.05 fA/sqrt(Hz) current noise and 200 nV/sqrt(Hz) voltage noise, both at 1 Hz, with an input impedance of 60 fF || 50 TOhm'. Optionally add: 'Commercial EEG front ends such as the TI ADS1299 do not specify current noise (300 pA typical input bias current, described as having negligible current noise); 1 fA/sqrt(Hz) is a modelling choice.'
bibliographic_issues: None. IEEE Journal on Emerging and Selected Topics in Circuits and Systems 1(4):526-535, December 2011, doi:10.1109/JETCAS.2011.2179419 - all match the IEEE record (ISSN 2156-3357).
